learning_objectives: Draw plan diagrams of transverse sections of herbaceous dicotyledonous stems, roots and leaves.
Describe the distribution of xylem and phloem in these transverse sections.
Draw and label xylem vessel elements, phloem sieve tube elements and companion cells.
Relate the structure of xylem vessel elements, sieve tube elements and companion cells to their functions.

sections.heading: Why plants need transport tissues
sections.body: A flowering plant has roots and leaves spread over a large volume. Water and mineral ions are absorbed mainly by roots, while sugars and amino acids are produced in photosynthetic or other metabolic tissues. Diffusion alone is too slow to move materials over the distances found in a large plant. Xylem transports water and dissolved mineral ions; phloem transports organic assimilates such as sucrose and amino acids in water. The tissues form continuous transport pathways through roots, stems and leaves.

sections.heading: Plan diagrams are tissue maps, not cell drawings
sections.body: A plan diagram shows the distribution and relative arrangement of tissues in a transverse section. Use clear, single lines, no shading, and label tissue regions with straight ruled label lines that do not cross. Show the overall outline and major tissue boundaries in proportion. Do not draw individual cells in a plan diagram. A detailed biological drawing is different: it shows the shape and arrangement of individual cells or structures at higher magnification.

sections.heading: Dicotyledonous stem in transverse section
sections.body: In a typical herbaceous dicotyledonous stem, vascular bundles are arranged in a ring near the outside of the stem. In each bundle, xylem is on the inner side, towards the centre of the stem, and phloem is on the outer side, towards the epidermis. A cambium may be present between xylem and phloem, but do not add it unless it is visible or required by the specimen. The ground tissue inside the ring is mainly pith; cortex lies between the vascular bundles and the epidermis.

sections.heading: Dicotyledonous root in transverse section
sections.body: In a typical herbaceous dicotyledonous root, the central vascular cylinder contains a star-shaped or cross-shaped xylem arrangement. Phloem occurs in groups between the arms of the xylem. The endodermis forms a boundary around the vascular cylinder, with cortex outside it and the epidermis at the surface. Identify the pattern rather than assuming every specimen has identical proportions.

sections.heading: Dicotyledonous leaf in transverse section
sections.body: A leaf vascular bundle is found in the vein or midrib. In a typical dicot leaf, xylem is towards the upper epidermis and phloem towards the lower epidermis. The upper and lower epidermises enclose mesophyll: palisade mesophyll is usually towards the upper surface and spongy mesophyll contains air spaces. A plan diagram should show tissue distribution and the position of the vascular bundle, not individual chloroplasts or every mesophyll cell.

sections.heading: Xylem vessel elements: structure fits water transport
sections.body: Xylem vessel elements are dead at functional maturity and joined end to end to form a continuous hollow vessel. End walls are absent or perforated, reducing resistance to water flow. The cell walls are thickened with lignin, which strengthens and waterproofs them and helps prevent collapse under the tension created by transpiration. Pits are regions without lignin where water can move sideways between vessels and surrounding cells. Lignin may be deposited in rings, spirals or a more continuous pattern.

sections.heading: Phloem sieve tube elements and companion cells
sections.body: Sieve tube elements are living cells joined end to end. Their end walls form sieve plates with pores that allow phloem sap to pass between elements. At maturity, sieve tube elements have very little cytoplasm and no nucleus, reducing resistance to mass flow. Companion cells are closely associated with sieve tube elements and contain a nucleus, dense cytoplasm and many mitochondria. Plasmodesmata connect the two cell types. Companion cells provide metabolic support and are involved in loading and unloading assimilates.

sections.heading: Relating tissue structure to function
sections.body: Xylem vessels provide a low-resistance pathway for water and dissolved mineral ions and resist collapse under tension because of lignified walls. Sieve tube elements provide a pathway for assimilates; sieve plates permit flow between elements, while reduced internal contents lower resistance. Companion cells contain many mitochondria to supply ATP for active transport processes and are linked to sieve tubes by plasmodesmata. In answers, link each named feature to a specific functional consequence.

questions.question: Describe the distribution of vascular bundles and the relative positions of xylem and phloem in a transverse section of a herbaceous dicotyledonous stem.
questions.answer: Vascular bundles form a ring near the outside of the stem. Xylem is on the inner side of each bundle, towards the centre; phloem is on the outer side, towards the epidermis.
mark_points: Vascular bundles arranged in a ring
Xylem towards the centre / inner side
Phloem towards the epidermis / outer side

questions.question: Describe the arrangement of xylem and phloem in a transverse section of a typical herbaceous dicotyledonous root.
questions.answer: Xylem is central and commonly forms a star or cross. Phloem occurs in groups between the arms of the xylem. The vascular cylinder is surrounded by the endodermis.

questions.question: State the relative positions of xylem and phloem in a typical dicotyledonous leaf vascular bundle.
questions.answer: Xylem is towards the upper epidermis and phloem is towards the lower epidermis.

questions.question: Explain three ways in which the structure of a xylem vessel element is adapted to its function.
questions.answer: Vessel elements are dead and hollow, forming a low-resistance continuous tube. Perforated or absent end walls allow water to pass between elements. Lignified walls strengthen the vessel and prevent collapse under tension; pits allow lateral water movement.
mark_points: Dead / no cytoplasm creates hollow lumen
End walls absent or perforated for flow
Lignified walls strengthen and prevent collapse

questions.question: Describe two structural differences between a sieve tube element and a companion cell.
questions.answer: A sieve tube element has sieve plates and, at maturity, lacks a nucleus and has little cytoplasm. A companion cell has a nucleus, dense cytoplasm and many mitochondria.
mark_points: Sieve tube has sieve plate; companion cell does not
Sieve tube lacks nucleus at maturity; companion cell has nucleus
Companion cell has many mitochondria / dense cytoplasm

questions.question: Explain how companion cells support translocation in phloem.
questions.answer: Companion cells provide metabolic support to sieve tube elements and use ATP in assimilate loading processes. Plasmodesmata connect companion cells to sieve tube elements, allowing substances and signals to pass between them.
mark_points: ATP supplies energy for loading processes
Plasmodesmata connect the two cell types
